cards.front: An {{c1::organelle}} is a small part inside a cell that does a special job.
cards.quote: An organelle is a small part inside a cell that does a special job.
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: Which cell part holds the instructions that guide what the cell makes and does?
cards.quote: Nucleus: holds the instructions that guide what the cell makes and does.
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: What two jobs does the cell membrane do?
cards.back: It controls what enters and leaves the cell, and it lets the cell sense its surroundings.
cards.quote: Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves, and lets the cell sense its surroundings.
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: What do mitochondria do for a cell?
cards.back: They release much of the energy stored in food, such as sugar (glucose) and fats, in a form the cell can use.
cards.quote: Mitochondria: release much of the energy stored in food such as sugar (glucose) and fats, in a form the cell can use.
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: What does the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) do?
cards.back: Its folded membranes help make and move many proteins and fats.
cards.quote: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): folded membranes that help make and move many proteins and fats.
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: What does a vacuole store?
cards.back: Water, food and wastes. Many animal cells have only small sacs instead.
cards.quote: Vacuole: stores water, food and wastes. Many animal cells have only small sacs
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: Name one kind of human cell that, when mature, has no nucleus and no mitochondria.
cards.back: A mature red blood cell. Not every cell has every part.
cards.quote: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus and no mitochondria.
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: Name the cell parts that help with making molecules, and say what each one adds.
cards.back: The nucleus gives the instructions, the ER helps make and move proteins and fats, and many reactions happen in the cytoplasm.
cards.why: Each organelle has a special job, and each job of the cell uses several organelles.
cards.quote: Key idea: Each organelle has a special job, and each job of the cell uses several organelles.
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: In a model heart muscle cell, you switch off the mitochondria. Predict what happens to growth, repair and the other life processes, and why.
cards.back: Many of them slow down. Growth, repair and other jobs need the energy that mitochondria release, and the parts work as one system.
cards.quote: Key idea: Organelles work as one system, so trouble in one part slows many life processes.
cards.section: Explain: the parts work as a team

cards.front: In 1968, scientists used chemicals to stop energy release in the mitochondria of guinea pig pancreas slices. What happened, and what does it show?
cards.back: New proteins made for export got stuck in the ER and could not move on toward the cell's exit. It shows that moving new proteins on from the ER depended on energy released by mitochondria: the parts work as a team.
cards.quote: chemicals that stopped energy release in the mitochondria left new proteins made for export stuck in the ER
cards.section: Explain: the parts work as a team

cards.front: In a cell using oxygen, how does gas exchange work?
cards.back: Oxygen moves in across the cell membrane, and carbon dioxide moves out. The mitochondria use the oxygen.
cards.quote: In a cell using oxygen, oxygen moves in across the cell membrane, and carbon dioxide moves out.
cards.section: Explain: the parts work as a team

cards.front: How does a cell respond to its environment?
cards.back: A signal reaches the cell, often at the cell membrane, and the cell changes what it makes or does.
cards.quote: A signal reaches the cell, often at the cell membrane, and the cell changes what it makes or does.
cards.section: Explain: the parts work as a team

cards.front: What does metabolism mean, and what are two key examples?
cards.back: All the chemical reactions inside the cell, building molecules up and breaking them down. Examples: photosynthesis (light used to make sugar) and cellular respiration (sugar broken down to release energy).
cards.quote: Metabolism means all the chemical reactions inside the cell, such as building molecules up and breaking them down.
cards.section: Explain: the parts work as a team

cards.front: A guinea pig pancreas cell builds digestive enzymes (proteins) and sends them out. Heart muscle mitochondria fill 22% to 37% of the cell. Predict whether the pancreas cell's share is as large, and why.
cards.back: Less: about 8.1%, below the whole heart range. Its job leans on making and moving protein, so rough ER filled about 22% of these cells.
cards.quote: Less: about 8.1%, below the whole heart range. Its job leans on making and moving protein,

cards.front: Mitochondria filled 9.0% of arm muscle and 8.6% of leg muscle in elite skiers. Find the mean, and compare it with the heart muscle range of 22% to 37%.
cards.back: (9.0 + 8.6) / 2 = 8.8%. That is lower than the whole heart range.
cards.quote: Find the mean of the two skier values (add them, then divide by 2).

cards.front: Mitochondria filled 34.5% of hummingbird flight muscle and about 0.7% of a chicken embryo white fat cell. How many percentage points apart are they?
cards.why: A percentage point is one step on the percent scale, so you subtract the two percents.
cards.quote: one percentage point is one step on the percent scale, such as 8% to 9%

cards.front: You test whether the spacing of a counting grid changes the measured share of a cell filled by mitochondria. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and the control.
cards.back: Independent: spacing between grid points (such as 10, 5 and 2 mm). Dependent: percent of points that land on mitochondria. Control: the finest grid (2 mm).
cards.quote: Independent variable: spacing between grid points, such as 10 mm, 5 mm and 2 mm.

cards.front: In a model cell, you switch off the cell membrane. Using the jobs of the membrane, predict which life processes suffer, and why.
cards.back: Gas exchange, removing wastes and response suffer. The membrane lets oxygen in and carbon dioxide out, controls what enters and leaves, and is often where signals reach the cell.
cards.why: Rests on the membrane's jobs and on the rule that organelles work as one system.
cards.quote: Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves, and lets the cell sense its surroundings.
cards.section: Explain: the parts and their jobs

cards.front: Heart muscle cells hold far more mitochondria than white fat cells. Why can that comparison not prove that every cell's job sets its parts?
cards.back: Two examples show a pattern, not a rule. A part's size alone does not tell you a cell's job, and a table of different cells cannot show what caused the difference.
cards.quote: Heart and fat cells show a pattern, not a rule: a part's size alone does not tell you a cell's job.

cards.front: In white fat cells, fat droplets filled about 90.9% and mitochondria about 0.7%. In the part that is not fat, about what share do mitochondria fill?
cards.back: 100 - 90.9 = 9.1% is not fat. 0.7 / 9.1 is about 7.7%, close to the pancreas cell's 8%. So the tiny share mostly reflects the fat taking the space.
cards.why: A rough estimate that assumes both numbers come from the same cells.
cards.quote: The part that is not fat is about 9.1% of the cell, and 0.7 out of 9.1 is about 7.7%.
